content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), commonly referred to as autism, is a developmental condition that typically begins in childhood and affects approximately 1% to 2% of children. It is characterized by difficulties in social communication, as well as repetitive and restricted behaviors and routines. These symptoms can negatively impact a child’s quality of life, academic performance, and social interactions. Memantine, a drug traditionally used to treat dementia, has been hypothesized to potentially reduce the core symptoms of autism, such as social communication difficulties and stereotypical behaviors, as well as co-occurring symptoms like hyperactivity and language impairments. However, it is essential to evaluate the evidence regarding its effectiveness in treating these symptoms. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of memantine on the core symptoms of autism, including social communication deficits and repetitive behaviors, as well as its impact on secondary outcomes such as language, memory, adaptive behavior, hyperactivity, and irritability. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, up to February 2022. Reference lists of key studies were reviewed, and experts in the field were consulted for additional relevant studies. Retraction databases were also checked, and no retractions or corrections were identified. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing memantine to placebo in individuals with autism. Trials in which both groups received the same additional therapy (e.g., behavioral intervention) but only one group received memantine were also included. Three RCTs were identified, involving a total of 204 participants. Two of these studies were conducted in the United States, and one was conducted in Iran. All studies focused on children and adolescents, with an average age of 9.4 years. The majority of participants were male (ranging from 73% to 87% across studies). The diagnosis of ASD was confirmed using established diagnostic tools, such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R). Memantine dosages ranged from 3 mg to 15 mg per day, adjusted based on the child’s weight. Two studies compared memantine to placebo, while the third study involved both groups receiving a behavioral intervention, with only one group also receiving memantine. All three studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias. One study was funded by Forest Laboratories, LLC, and the sponsor was involved in various aspects of the study, including design, data collection, and analysis. The other two studies reported no financial support, although one received the study medication as an in-kind contribution from Forest Pharmaceuticals. Regarding the primary outcomes, there was no clear evidence that memantine reduced the severity of core autism symptoms compared to placebo. The standardized mean difference in autism symptom scores between the intervention and control groups was –0.74 standard deviations (95% confidence interval: −2.07 to 0.58), based on very low-certainty evidence. Additionally, two studies (144 participants) reported adverse effects potentially related to the treatment, but there was no significant difference in adverse effects between the memantine and placebo groups (odds ratio: 0.64, 95% confidence interval: 0.17 to 2.39; low-certainty evidence). For secondary outcomes, there was no evidence of a difference between memantine and placebo in terms of language abilities (2 studies, 144 participants; low-certainty evidence), memory or adaptive behavior (1 study, 23 participants; both low-certainty evidence), or hyperactivity and irritability (1 study, 121 participants; both low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, it remains unclear whether memantine is an effective treatment for children with autism. None of the included studies evaluated the effects of memantine in adults with autism. Further research with more rigorous study designs, larger sample sizes, longer follow-up periods, and outcome measures that are meaningful to autistic individuals and their families is needed to better understand the potential role of memantine in treating autism.
